triage.name: Optic neuritis
triage.reason: Subacute monocular vision loss with pain on eye movement; classic neuro-ophthalmology case with strong link to demyelinating disease and clear look-alikes.

presentation: term "Uhthoff's phenomenon" not found in SNOMED CT
exam: term 'Extraocular movement abnormality' not found in SNOMED CT
exam: term 'Cranial nerve deficit' not found in SNOMED CT

demographics: More common in women, roughly 2–3 times more often than men
More common in people of Northern European ancestry
Uncommon in children and in adults over 50

risk_factors.text: Known multiple sclerosis or a prior episode of demyelinating disease
Recent viral illness or upper respiratory infection

comorbidities: Other autoimmune disease such as systemic lupus erythematosus or Sjögren syndrome
family_history: Multiple sclerosis in a first-degree relative
Other autoimmune disease in the family
social_history: No consistent association with smoking, alcohol or occupation

chief_complaints.text: My vision in one eye went blurry
It hurts behind my eye when I move it
Colors look washed out and dull in that eye

hpi.onset: Subacute, developing over hours to a few days
hpi.duration: Typically 1–7 days at presentation, with visual loss reaching its worst within about 1–2 weeks
hpi.progression: Vision worsens over several days, then plateaus; spontaneous improvement usually begins within 2–3 weeks and continues over months
hpi.location: One eye, often described as behind or around the eye
hpi.radiation: Pain may radiate to the brow or temple on the same side
hpi.quality: Vision is blurred, foggy or washed out; pain is dull and aching
hpi.severity: Vision ranges from mild blurring to marked loss; pain is usually mild to moderate, about 3–5/10
hpi.timing: Pain is worse with eye movement and is constant otherwise; vision is worse in heat or after exercise
aggravating: Heat, such as a hot shower or fever

associated_symptoms.text: Reduced color vision, colors look faded or washed out
Blurred or dim vision in the affected eye
Loss of part of the visual field, often central
Flashes of light with eye movement
Vision gets worse with heat or exercise
Numbness or tingling elsewhere on the body
Weakness in an arm or leg

pertinent_negatives: Severe constant eye pain with a red eye
Sudden painless loss of vision like a curtain coming down
Contact lens use with a painful red eye

positives.text: Colors look faded in the affected eye
Tingling or numbness in the limbs

argues_against: Focal weakness that is the main problem
Sinus or ear disease causing eye symptoms
Systemic lupus erythematosus with rash or oral ulcers

atypical.how_it_differs: Often bilateral, follows a recent infection or vaccination, and the child may not report pain or color changes; optic disc swelling is more common.
missing_classic_features: Clear report of pain with eye movement

atypical.how_it_differs: Vision loss is more often painless and bilateral, and ischemic or compressive causes are more likely than demyelination.
Optic neuritis can occur or flare in the postpartum period, and treatment options such as high-dose corticosteroids must be weighed against pregnancy risks.
missing_classic_features: Typical age and sex pattern may be shifted

atypical.how_it_differs: Infectious and infiltrative causes are more likely, and the course may be more severe or bilateral.

general.mild: Well-appearing, no distress; may squint or cover the affected eye
general.moderate: Mild discomfort with eye movement, otherwise well-appearing
general.severe: Visibly bothered by eye pain, avoids moving the affected eye, may hold the head still
general.critical: Rarely toxic-appearing; if present, consider an alternative diagnosis such as infection or a compressive lesion

findings.maneuver: Swing a bright light back and forth between the two eyes and compare the pupillary constriction
findings.finding: The affected pupil dilates rather than constricts when the light swings to it (Marcus Gunn pupil)

findings.maneuver: Check visual acuity in each eye separately with a Snellen chart or near card
findings.finding: Reduced visual acuity in the affected eye, ranging from mild blurring to counting fingers or worse

findings.maneuver: Test color vision in each eye with Ishihara plates or a red desaturation comparison
findings.finding: Colors appear washed out or less saturated in the affected eye, out of proportion to the acuity loss

findings.maneuver: Ask the patient to look up, down, left and right and report any pain
findings.finding: Retro-orbital or periorbital pain provoked by eye movement

findings.maneuver: Confrontational visual field testing in each eye
findings.finding: A central or paracentral scotoma in the affected eye

findings.maneuver: Direct ophthalmoscopy of the optic disc in each eye
findings.finding: Blurred disc margins with hyperemia and swelling (papillitis); the disc may be normal in retrobulbar neuritis

findings.maneuver: Inspect the conjunctiva and sclera in room light
findings.finding: No conjunctival injection or ciliary flush

findings.maneuver: Shine a light into each eye and ask about light sensitivity
Test extraocular movements in all directions of gaze
findings.finding: Full, conjugate movements without ophthalmoplegia or nystagmus

findings.maneuver: Screen cranial nerves II through XII
findings.finding: No cranial nerve deficit other than the affected optic nerve

findings.maneuver: Test strength in the arms and legs
Test deep tendon reflexes at the biceps, brachioradialis, patella and Achilles
findings.finding: Normal symmetric reflexes; hyperreflexia may suggest prior demyelinating disease

findings.maneuver: Test light touch and pinprick in the limbs and trunk
findings.finding: No sensory level or focal sensory loss

findings.maneuver: Observe the patient walking and turning
Flex the neck and check for resistance

labs.caveat: Nonspecific; a markedly elevated ESR with severe vision loss should raise concern for giant cell arteritis or another inflammatory optic neuropathy.
Usually normal or only mildly elevated in demyelinating optic neuritis; a high value points away from typical optic neuritis.
Thyroid eye disease can cause optic neuropathy; check when there is proptosis, lid retraction or a history of thyroid disease.
B12 deficiency can cause bilateral optic neuropathy; consider when vision loss is bilateral or there is a sensory neuropathy.
Consider alongside B12 in nutritional or malabsorptive states.
Negative. Required in anyone who could be pregnant before MRI with gadolinium or high-dose corticosteroids.
Mildly elevated opening pressure can occur; marked elevation suggests raised intracranial pressure rather than optic neuritis.
Mild lymphocytic pleocytosis is typical of demyelinating disease; a high count or neutrophil predominance suggests infection.
Mildly elevated protein is common; very high protein suggests an alternative cause.
Low CSF glucose is not typical of optic neuritis and should prompt evaluation for infection or malignancy.

imaging.study: MRI brain and orbits with and without IV gadolinium
imaging.preferred_when: All patients with suspected optic neuritis; the key test to confirm the diagnosis and assess demyelinating disease burden

findings.text: T2 hyperintensity and gadolinium enhancement of the affected optic nerve
Periventricular, juxtacortical, infratentorial or spinal cord T2 lesions consistent with demyelinating disease
Normal optic nerve and brain (does not exclude optic neuritis, especially early or with mild disease)

imaging.preferred_when: Pregnancy or when gadolinium is contraindicated; less sensitive for acute optic nerve enhancement

findings.text: T2 hyperintense white matter lesions suggesting demyelinating disease

imaging.study: Optical coherence tomography (OCT) of the optic nerve
imaging.preferred_when: Adjunct to assess retinal nerve fiber layer thickness and detect subclinical optic nerve damage

findings.text: Thinning of the retinal nerve fiber layer in the affected eye, often after recovery
Normal retinal nerve fiber layer early in the course

imaging.study: CT head and orbits without contrast
imaging.preferred_when: When MRI is unavailable or contraindicated, or to exclude a mass or hemorrhage in an atypical presentation

findings.text: Usually normal; may show optic nerve enlargement

initial.test: MRI brain and orbits with and without IV gadolinium
initial.why: Confirms optic nerve inflammation and looks for demyelinating lesions that predict multiple sclerosis
Rules out pregnancy before gadolinium or high-dose corticosteroids
Screens for giant cell arteritis in older adults with severe vision loss
initial.only_if: age over 50 with severe or painless vision loss

initial.why: Supports concern for giant cell arteritis or another inflammatory cause
initial.only_if: age over 50 with severe or painless vision loss

supporting.test: Optical coherence tomography (OCT) of the optic nerve
supporting.why: Quantifies retinal nerve fiber layer loss and supports the diagnosis
Evaluates for infection, inflammation or oligoclonal bands when the diagnosis is uncertain or atypical
supporting.only_if: atypical features, suspected infection, or need to distinguish from neuromyelitis optica

supporting.why: Screens for thyroid eye disease when proptosis or lid findings are present
supporting.only_if: proptosis, lid retraction or known thyroid disease

supporting.why: Evaluates for nutritional optic neuropathy when vision loss is bilateral or there is a sensory neuropathy
supporting.only_if: bilateral involvement or suspected nutritional deficiency

not_indicated.why: Routine blood count is not needed to diagnose optic neuritis
Metabolic panel is not routinely helpful

not_indicated.test: ct head and orbits without contrast
not_indicated.why: MRI is more sensitive for optic nerve and brain demyelination; CT is reserved for when MRI is unavailable or contraindicated

decision_points: Pregnancy test before gadolinium MRI or high-dose corticosteroids in anyone who could be pregnant
In adults over 50 with severe or painless vision loss, consider giant cell arteritis and start high-dose corticosteroids immediately rather than waiting for biopsy
Atypical features such as bilateral involvement, severe persistent pain, no light perception, or lack of recovery should prompt evaluation for neuromyelitis optica, infection, or compressive causes
MRI findings of demyelinating lesions change the risk of developing multiple sclerosis and guide referral to neurology

differential.name: Giant cell arteritis
differential.why_considered: Older adult with sudden or severe vision loss, sometimes with eye or head pain
differential.trigger: Age over 50 with new vision loss, headache, jaw claudication, or scalp tenderness

history: New headache, scalp tenderness, or jaw pain with chewing
Constitutional symptoms such as fever, weight loss, or malaise
Vision loss may be painless and severe
exam: Tender, nodular, or pulseless temporal artery
Normal pain with eye movement is often absent
imaging: Temporal artery ultrasound showing halo sign
Temporal artery biopsy showing granulomatous inflammation

differential.name: Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder
differential.why_considered: Optic neuritis that is severe, bilateral, or recurrent, especially with other neurologic symptoms
differential.trigger: Bilateral or severe optic neuritis with longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis or area postrema syndrome

history: Severe vision loss, often worse than typical optic neuritis
Bilateral eye involvement at onset or recurrent episodes
Weakness, numbness, or bladder dysfunction from transverse myelitis
exam: Severe visual acuity loss, often worse than 20/200
Sensory level or paraparesis from myelitis
labs: CSF may show pleocytosis without oligoclonal bands
imaging: Longitudinally extensive optic nerve lesion on MRI
Longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis on spinal MRI

differential.name: Ischemic optic neuropathy
differential.why_considered: Sudden painless monocular vision loss with optic disc swelling, especially in older adults
differential.trigger: Sudden painless vision loss with a swollen optic disc in a patient over 50

history: Sudden onset, often noticed on waking
History of hypertension, diabetes, or sleep apnea
exam: Diffuse or sectoral optic disc swelling
labs: ESR and CRP normal or only mildly elevated
imaging: MRI optic nerve usually normal or shows mild swelling without enhancement

differential.name: Papilledema from raised intracranial pressure
differential.why_considered: Bilateral optic disc swelling with visual symptoms and headache
differential.trigger: Bilateral disc swelling with headache, transient visual obscurations, or pulsatile tinnitus

history: Headache worse lying down or on waking
Transient visual obscurations with postural change
imaging: MRI brain with empty sella, flattened posterior globes, or optic nerve sheath distension
MR venography to exclude venous sinus thrombosis

differential.name: Compressive optic neuropathy
differential.why_considered: Progressive monocular vision loss with optic disc swelling or pallor
differential.trigger: Progressive painless vision loss with proptosis, diplopia, or no recovery

labs: Thyroid function tests if thyroid eye disease suspected
imaging: MRI or CT showing a mass, meningioma, or enlarged extraocular muscles compressing the optic nerve

differential.name: Central serous chorioretinopathy
differential.why_considered: Central vision blurring and color changes in one eye

history: Often in younger to middle-aged adults under stress or using corticosteroids
exam: Reduced central vision with a relative scotoma
No afferent pupillary defect or mild only
Subretinal fluid on dilated fundus exam

differential.name: Vitreous hemorrhage
differential.why_considered: Sudden painless monocular vision loss with floaters

history: History of diabetes, trauma, or retinal tear
exam: Blood in the vitreous on fundoscopy

differential.name: Retinal detachment
differential.why_considered: Sudden painless vision loss with flashes and floaters

history: Sudden onset of flashes and floaters
exam: Visual field defect respecting the horizontal meridian
Retinal tear or detachment on dilated fundoscopy

history: Associated autoimmune disease or recent trauma
exam: Cells and flare in the anterior chamber
labs: HLA-B27 or autoimmune workup if recurrent

differential.name: Leber hereditary optic neuropathy
differential.why_considered: Subacute painless bilateral vision loss in a young adult

history: Maternal family history of vision loss
exam: Optic disc hyperemia and telangiectatic vessels early
labs: Mitochondrial DNA mutations on genetic testing

severity.mild: Mild blurring and color desaturation in one eye, pain with eye movement, visual acuity 20/40 or better, able to read and drive
severity.moderate: Visual acuity between 20/50 and 20/200, obvious color vision loss, pain with eye movement, difficulty reading or recognizing faces
severity.severe: Visual acuity worse than 20/200, dense central scotoma, marked pain, unable to read or navigate, may have no light perception in severe cases

red_flags.finding: Age over 50 with new severe or painless vision loss
red_flags.meaning: Consider giant cell arteritis; start high-dose corticosteroids immediately to prevent fellow eye involvement
Consider neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder, Leber hereditary optic neuropathy, or toxic/nutritional optic neuropathy

red_flags.finding: No light perception in the affected eye
red_flags.meaning: Atypical for demyelinating optic neuritis; consider severe neuromyelitis optica, compression, or ischemia

red_flags.finding: Proptosis, ophthalmoplegia, or cranial nerve deficits
red_flags.meaning: Suggests a compressive or infiltrative lesion rather than demyelinating optic neuritis

red_flags.finding: Fever, neck stiffness, or severe headache
red_flags.meaning: Consider infection or raised intracranial pressure rather than optic neuritis

red_flags.finding: Vision loss that continues to worsen beyond 2 weeks or fails to improve by 4–6 weeks
red_flags.meaning: Atypical course; reconsider the diagnosis and evaluate for alternative causes

complications.name: Persistent visual impairment
clues: Incomplete recovery of visual acuity or color vision
Thinning of the retinal nerve fiber layer on OCT

complications.name: Development of multiple sclerosis
clues: White matter lesions on MRI at presentation
New neurologic symptoms over months to years

complications.name: Recurrent optic neuritis
clues: New episode of pain with eye movement and vision loss in either eye

complications.name: Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder
clues: Transverse myelitis with sensory level or paraparesis

special_populations.differences: Often bilateral, follows a recent infection or vaccination, and the child may not report pain or color changes; optic disc swelling is more common. Recovery is generally good but the risk of subsequent demyelinating disease remains.
Vision loss is more often painless and bilateral, and ischemic or compressive causes are more likely than demyelination. Giant cell arteritis must be excluded urgently with ESR and CRP.
Optic neuritis can occur or flare in the postpartum period. MRI without gadolinium is preferred when possible, and high-dose corticosteroids must be weighed against pregnancy risks.
Infectious and infiltrative causes are more likely, and the course may be more severe or bilateral. A lower threshold for CSF studies and imaging is warranted.

key_questions.question: Which eye is affected, and how did the vision change start?
key_questions.looking_for: Monocular, subacute blurring or dimming over hours to a few days

key_questions.question: Does it hurt when you move your eye?
key_questions.looking_for: Retro-orbital or periorbital pain provoked by eye movement

key_questions.question: Do colors look different between the two eyes?
key_questions.looking_for: Washed-out or desaturated color vision in the affected eye, out of proportion to acuity loss

key_questions.question: Is the vision getting worse, staying the same, or improving?
key_questions.looking_for: Worsening over several days then plateau; improvement usually begins within 2–3 weeks

key_questions.question: Does heat or exercise make the vision worse?
key_questions.looking_for: Uhthoff phenomenon, transient worsening with heat or exertion

key_questions.question: Any numbness, tingling, weakness, or trouble with balance or bladder control?
key_questions.looking_for: Other neurologic symptoms suggesting demyelinating disease or neuromyelitis optica

key_questions.question: Have you had episodes like this before?
key_questions.looking_for: Prior optic neuritis or known multiple sclerosis

key_questions.question: Have you ever been diagnosed with multiple sclerosis or another autoimmune disease?
Do you take any medications, especially ethambutol, isoniazid, amiodarone, or a TNF inhibitor?
key_questions.looking_for: Toxic optic neuropathy from a culprit medication

key_questions.question: Does anyone in your family have multiple sclerosis or other autoimmune disease?
key_questions.looking_for: Family history of demyelinating or autoimmune disease

key_questions.question: Have you had a recent viral illness, upper respiratory infection, or vaccination?
key_questions.looking_for: Recent infection or vaccination as a trigger

key_questions.question: Is the pain severe and constant, or is the eye red, or is there discharge?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; a painful red eye suggests uveitis, keratitis, or angle-closure glaucoma instead

key_questions.question: Did the vision loss come on suddenly and painlessly, like a curtain coming down?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; sudden painless loss suggests ischemia, retinal detachment, or vitreous hemorrhage

key_questions.question: How old are you, and have you had headaches, scalp tenderness, or jaw pain with chewing?
key_questions.looking_for: Age over 50 with cranial symptoms suggesting giant cell arteritis

reasoning_points: Subacute monocular vision loss developing over hours to a few days
Retro-orbital or periorbital pain provoked by eye movement
Reduced color vision or red desaturation out of proportion to acuity loss
Afferent pupillary defect (Marcus Gunn pupil) in the affected eye
Visual field defect, typically a central or paracentral scotoma
Optic disc may be normal (retrobulbar neuritis) or swollen (papillitis)
No red eye, discharge, or photophobia to suggest intraocular disease
MRI brain and orbits showing optic nerve T2 hyperintensity and gadolinium enhancement, with or without demyelinating white matter lesions
Alternative causes such as giant cell arteritis, neuromyelitis optica, ischemia, compression, and toxic or nutritional optic neuropathy considered and excluded

easy: Young woman with unilateral subacute blurring and pain on eye movement
Red desaturation and an afferent pupillary defect on exam
No red eye and no other neurologic findings
medium: Optic disc appears normal (retrobulbar neuritis) so the fundus exam is not obviously abnormal
Pain is mild or attributed to sinus or eye strain
Patient reports only color changes or a central scotoma rather than frank vision loss
MRI shows demyelinating white matter lesions raising the question of multiple sclerosis
hard: Older adult with painless severe vision loss where giant cell arteritis must be excluded urgently
Bilateral or recurrent severe optic neuritis suggesting neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder
Progressive painless vision loss with proptosis or cranial nerve deficits suggesting a compressive lesion
Bilateral painless vision loss in a young adult suggesting Leber hereditary optic neuropathy or a toxic/nutritional cause
Patient on ethambutol, isoniazid, amiodarone, or a TNF inhibitor where toxic optic neuropathy is the alternative
